summary: This paper introduces Concept Distributed Alignment Search (CDAS), a model steering approach that combines Distributed Interchange Interventions (DII) with full-vocabulary Jensen-Shannon Divergence distribution matching. The method is evaluated on general concept steering via AXBENCH as well as two safety-critical case studies: overriding refusal in safety-aligned LLMs up to 70B parameters and neutralizing chain-of-thought backdoors. CDAS demonstrates strong utility preservation and low distribution shift in safety concept suppression, though its general steering performance is layer-sensitive and heavily reliant on inference-time factor tuning.
strengths: Principled formulation combining causal interchange interventions (DII) with full-vocabulary distribution matching (JSD), shifting model steering from reward/likelihood maximization toward internal feature consistency.

Strong empirical performance on safety concept suppression across large models (up to Llama-3.1-70B), achieving high refusal overriding while maintaining general benchmark capabilities (MMLU/TruthfulQA) and low KL divergence.
Effective defense in chain-of-thought backdoor neutralization, outperforming baselines on unseen trigger prompts with minimal impact on standard benchmarks.
Transparent self-assessment of limitations, including discussion of training data requirements, factor tuning needs, and restriction to rank-1 interventions.

key_concerns.issue: Gap between theoretical motivation and empirical findings regarding factor tuning: while DII is motivated as naturally sampling steering factors on-distribution without manual tuning, CDAS with unit factors fails severely on AXBENCH (0.121–0.238), requiring manual factor tuning to achieve competitive performance.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Clarify this discrepancy in the main text and discuss why unit factors succeed in safety suppression but fail in general concept elicitation.

key_concerns.issue: Anomalous baseline performance for RePS in refusal suppression: RePS suffers a catastrophic drop of ~35% on MMLU and ~27% on TruthfulQA on Llama-3.1-8B, alongside 0% refusal suppression, suggesting potential hyperparameter misconfiguration or tuning issues.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Re-evaluate the hyperparameter search for RePS on Llama models to ensure a fair comparison, or explain the root cause of this severe baseline collapse.

key_concerns.issue: Lack of reported variance and error bounds across tabular results: Tables 1, 2, 3, and 4 report single point estimates without standard deviations, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Provide standard deviations or standard errors across random splits and seeds for all benchmark tables.

questions_for_authors: Why does the unit factor (beta=1) work effectively for refusal suppression and backdoor neutralization, but perform poorly on general concept steering in AXBENCH?
Could you provide additional details on the hyperparameter search and failure analysis for RePS on Llama-3.1-8B/70B during refusal suppression?
How sensitive is CDAS performance to the choice of token position within the model chat template tokens across different architectures?
calibration_check: The claims are generally well-scoped, as the authors explicitly note limitations regarding factor tuning, data requirements, and layer sensitivity, although the initial motivation framing DII as eliminating factor predesignation is somewhat contradicted by AXBENCH results.

significance.justification: Addresses important challenges in lightweight LLM steering and safety control, though practical impact on general concept steering is tempered by layer sensitivity and factor tuning needs.

novelty.justification: Offers an original synthesis of causal variable localization (DII) and full-vocabulary Jensen-Shannon Divergence distribution matching for model steering.

rigor.justification: The objective derivation and experimental setups are sound, but anomalous baseline collapses (RePS) and dependency on factor tuning warrant closer refinement.

statistical_soundness.justification: AXBENCH uses 10-split averages and Figure 1 includes error bands, but standard deviations and significance testing are missing across all main tables.

calibration_honesty.justification: The authors are candid about limitations and negative results, though the framing of DII as tuning-free is partially contradicted by AXBENCH experiments.

clarity.justification: The manuscript is well-written, logically structured, and clearly presents mathematical definitions and experimental methodologies.

structure_compliance.justification: Strictly adheres to standard conference formatting with appropriate sections, figure/table captions, and appendices.

reproducibility.justification: Hyperparameters, model layers, training objectives, and data curation procedures are described in sufficient detail to enable reproduction.

related_work.justification: Accurately contextualizes the approach within model steering, mechanistic interpretability, distribution matching, and safety analysis.

figure_quality.justification: Table and figure captions are descriptive, informative, and clearly convey the underlying experimental trends and metrics.

breadth_generality.justification: Evaluates general concepts on Gemma models and safety tasks on Phi/Llama models up to 70B, but is restricted to rank-1 steering vectors and selective layer choices.

overall_recommendation.justification: A solid, insightful paper combining distribution matching with causal interventions that excels at utility-preserving safety steering, though weak unit-factor performance on general steering holds it back from a strong accept.
